summary: Single-author study of four prompting conditions for spec-driven Python code generation. (A) traceSDD: a hierarchical REQ-XXX.Y.Z spec with mandatory per-line requirement-ID comments. (B) The same spec without comments. (C) Spec Kit-style prose specs. (D) OpenSpec-style specs with trace YAML. Three cold-start runs per condition, on 20 tasks with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and 50 different tasks with GLM-5-turbo. Per-line citations lower run-to-run lexical similarity compared with the same spec without citations. A grep for cited IDs absent from the spec catches 86-88% of hallucinations that were injected carrying fake IDs. Every condition passes 100% of its tests.

claims.claim: Mandatory per-line citations reduce output determinism relative to the identical uncited spec (Claude d about -0.73 to -0.76; GLM d=-0.72)
claims.evidence: Tables 1-2: paired t-tests, Wilcoxon, CIs. The uncited arm is a proper control. Determinism is difflib similarity on comment-stripped code from 3 runs (2 comparisons per task). The two models ran different task sets, so 'cross-model replication' also changes the tasks. The abstract gives d=-0.76, p=0.003 while Table 2 gives d=-0.73, p=0.004, and p=0.004 is starred '***'.

claims.claim: Only the cited condition enables automated hallucination detection: TDR 86.4-88.0% with 0% FPR, vs 0% for all alternatives
claims.evidence: Table 3. Per §4.4, the hallucinations were injected with fake IDs (REQ-099/098/097), so the orphan-ID check catches what was built to be caught. Organic hallucinations that cite a valid ID, and wrong-requirement citations, are never tested. The alternatives score 0% because no detector was run on them (their FPR is 'N/A'), not because an import allowlist, linter or spec review fails. §6.5 attributes misses to 'the LLM omitting the citation', which contradicts the manual-injection description.

claims.claim: traceSDD (cited) outperforms Spec Kit on determinism (pre-registered H1 supported)
claims.evidence: Table 2: d=0.47 (p=0.049) and d=0.42 (p=0.003), but the pre-registered criterion in §3 requires |d|>0.5, so H1 fails by the paper's own locked threshold even though the text calls it supported. Not significant vs OpenSpec. No registry link or timestamp is given for the pre-registration.

claims.claim: Citation discipline does not affect functional correctness (100% TPR in all conditions)
claims.evidence: §6.4. The result is at ceiling on 50-800-line Python tasks, and the number of tests per task is not reported. This cannot detect any effect.

claims.claim: A REQ-format spec without citations gives the best determinism anchor vs Spec Kit and OpenSpec (d about 1)
claims.evidence: Table 2. Spec Kit and OpenSpec arms are the author's renderings of their spec formats, not runs of the tools' workflows. Lexical similarity is not a quality measure.

patterns.note: Requirement-ID citations verified by an orphan-ID set difference. The comparison is a strawman: alternatives have no detector at all, and the 'hallucinations' are synthetic injections carrying fake IDs. Nothing verifies that a cited ID is the correct requirement or that the cited requirement is implemented. The measured cost is lower run-to-run lexical consistency (d about -0.72).

A hierarchical REQ-XXX.Y.Z format vs Spec Kit's prose user stories and acceptance criteria: the REQ format gives higher lexical consistency (uncited vs Spec Kit d=0.98-1.05). Correctness is at ceiling in every arm, and lexical similarity does not measure quality.
All four arms are spec-driven; the study compares spec formats and annotation, not spec-driven vs not.

methodology.sample: 70 author-built Python tasks (20 for Claude, 50 different ones for GLM); 4 conditions x 3 runs; 840 implementations
methodology.baselines: The same spec without citations (good control); Spec Kit and OpenSpec spec formats as rendered by the author
methodology.variance: SDs, t-intervals, bootstrap CIs, Holm correction; only 3 runs per cell
methodology.ablations: Cited vs uncited; difficulty and size subgroups (GLM)

standards.artifacts: None: tasks, specs, generated code and analysis scripts are not released
standards.preregistration: Claimed, but with no registry or timestamp, and the locked H1 threshold is not applied

biases.detail: The author built traceSDD (secondary summaries attribute it to Panda; the paper does not disclose this), wrote the tasks, and injected the hallucinations the detector is scored on.
Competing formats get TDR 0% because no detection mechanism was applied to them.
TDR is measured on synthetic fake-ID injections; lexical similarity is used as a stand-in for determinism or quality.
50-800-line utility and algorithm tasks with 100% pass in every arm.
Reference [8] (a study of casual OSS contributors) is cited as a traceability-tool survey, and [19] (Kaplan scaling laws) is cited for clone-detection similarity. The bibliography appears unchecked.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: traceSDD (apparently the author's own) vs GitHub Spec Kit and OpenSpec
coi.detail: A developer evaluates their own framework favourably against two public alternatives, using tasks and injected faults they constructed, with no independent replication. The paper does report a cost of its own method (lower determinism).

verdict_reason: One finding is defensible: requiring per-line requirement-ID comments changes the generated code and lowers run-to-run lexical similarity, compared with the same spec without them (paired, two models). The headline detection result is tautological on synthetic fake-ID injections against detector-less baselines. The pre-registered H1 fails its own threshold, nothing is released, and the bibliography contains miscitations.
applicability: Directly on topic for the team's spec-driven rollout, but the evidence is thin. What is safe to take: if specs carry stable requirement IDs and code or tests cite them, a CI check can flag citations to IDs that do not exist. That is cheap and deterministic, but it only catches fabricated IDs. It does not show that a cited requirement is implemented, and it misses out-of-scope code cited under a valid ID or left uncited. For the the repositories, put IDs on acceptance tests (JUnit @Tag or display names) and verify each link by running that test, rather than adding per-line comments. Do not adopt per-line citation on this paper's evidence.
